# Obama Shares Holiday Spirit with Troops in Hawaii

(CNN) -- President-elect Barack Obama paid a visit to military personnel and their families as they enjoyed Christmas dinner at a Marine Corps base in Hawaii on Thursday, taking a break from his holiday vacation to extend season's greetings to service members.

The president-elect traveled to Marine Corps Base Hawaii at Kaneohe Bay on Oahu, where he mingled warmly with Marines and sailors gathered for a traditional holiday meal featuring turkey, roast beef, ham, and all the seasonal trimmings.

Dressed casually in a blue polo shirt and dark khaki trousers, Obama moved easily through the dining hall—festively adorned with Christmas trees and Santa figurines—chatting with service members, shaking hands, and posing for photographs. Shortly before his arrival, a Marine addressed the crowd assembled at 25 tables, announcing, "You need to take your seats, the president-elect is going to be coming."

Over the course of about an hour, Obama worked his way methodically around the room, table by table, offering warm greetings along the way. "Just wanted to say, 'Hi, hey guys,'" he remarked at one stop, while at another he offered a simple, "Hey guys, Merry Christmas."

The visit coincided with a broader tribute to America's armed forces, as Obama's holiday message—set to air on radio Saturday and posted online Wednesday—paid homage to troops serving overseas. "As we celebrate this joyous time of year, our thoughts turn to the brave men and women who serve our country far from home," he said. "Their extraordinary and selfless sacrifice is an inspiration to us all, and part of the unbroken line of heroism that has made our freedom and prosperity possible for over two centuries."

Currently, more than 140,000 troops are stationed in Iraq, alongside roughly 30,000 in Afghanistan.

In his broadcast remarks, Obama also called on Americans to embrace a renewed sense of common purpose and shared citizenship, acknowledging the economic hardships facing many families. "These are also tough times for many Americans struggling in our sluggish economy," he said. "Now, more than ever, we must rededicate ourselves to the notion that we share a common destiny as Americans—that I am my brother's keeper, I am my sister's keeper. ... We must all do our part to serve one another; to seek new ideas and new innovation; and to start a new chapter for our great country."

This spirit of unity, Obama noted, would serve as a guiding principle for his incoming administration. "If the American people come together and put their shoulder to the wheel of history, then I know that we can put our people back to work ... and reach the promise of a brighter day."

This philosophy, Obama stated, would shape his administration's approach going forward. He expressed confidence that through collective effort and determination, Americans could restore employment opportunities and work toward a more hopeful future.

He acknowledged the significant economic challenges facing the nation, as many families continued to struggle amid a sluggish economy. # Obama Spends Christmas with Troops at Marine Corps Base Hawaii

President-elect Barack Obama took time out of his holiday vacation in Hawaii to visit with military service members and their families at Marine Corps Base Hawaii Kaneohe Bay on Christmas Day, marking a symbolic gesture of goodwill as he prepared to assume the presidency in the coming weeks.

Arriving at the base with his family, Obama joined troops and their loved ones for a traditional Christmas dinner, complete with all the trimmings typically associated with the holiday meal. Rather than maintaining the formal distance often expected of high-profile visitors, the president-elect moved easily among the tables, shaking hands, posing for photographs, and engaging in warm, casual conversation with service members and their spouses and children. Witnesses described the atmosphere as relaxed and genuine, with Obama taking a personal interest in hearing about the families' experiences and the challenges of military life, particularly for those with loved ones serving overseas.

Following the dinner, Obama delivered a special holiday radio address in which he paid tribute to the more than 170,000 American troops currently deployed in Iraq and Afghanistan. In his remarks, he acknowledged the profound sacrifices made by these service members and their families, many of whom were spending the holiday season separated from one another due to their commitments abroad. He expressed gratitude on behalf of the nation for their dedication and service during what he described as a critical and challenging time for the country.

The visit came at a pivotal moment in Obama's transition to the presidency, as he worked to establish connections with various constituencies ahead of his inauguration. By choosing to spend part of his Christmas holiday with military families rather than keeping the day entirely private, Obama sent a clear signal about the priority he intended to place on supporting the armed forces and their families throughout his administration.

The gesture also carried broader symbolic weight given the difficult economic circumstances facing the nation at the time. With many Americans grappling with job losses, financial insecurity, and uncertainty about the future amid a deepening recession, Obama's visit to Kaneohe Bay served as a reminder of shared sacrifice and collective purpose. By honoring the men and women in uniform who were spending the holidays away from home in service to their country, the president-elect sought to emphasize themes of unity and mutual responsibility that would become central to his approaching presidency.

The visit was widely covered by media outlets, who noted the informal and heartfelt nature of the president-elect's interactions with military families, contrasting with the more choreographed public appearances typical of political figures. Analysts suggested that such moments helped humanize Obama to the public and reinforced his commitment to supporting troops and veterans as he prepared to take on the responsibilities of commander-in-chief.
